questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute the magnitude of a gradient vector
questions.stem: A field is given by f of x comma y comma z equal to x squared plus y squared plus z squared. What is the magnitude of the gradient of f at the point (1, 2, 3)? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The gradient collects the three partial derivatives, which are 2x, 2y and 2z, so at (1, 2, 3) it is <2, 4, 6> and its magnitude is the square root of 4 + 16 + 36 = 56, about 7.4833. That magnitude is the steepest rate of increase of f per unit distance, which is why it is worth computing rather than reading a single component. Summing the components to get 12, or keeping the squared magnitude 56, each answer a different question about the same vector.
questions.hint: Collect the three partial derivatives, then take the magnitude of the resulting vector.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a directional derivative from the gradient
questions.stem: Let f of x comma y equal to x squared plus 3xy, and let u be the unit vector with both components equal to 1 over the square root of 2. What is the directional derivative of f in the direction u at the point (1, 3)? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The directional derivative is the gradient dotted with the unit direction, and the gradient here is <2x + 3y, 3x> which at (1, 3) is <11, 3>. Dotting with the unit vector gives (11 + 3) over the square root of 2, that is 14 over the square root of 2, which is 7 times the square root of 2, about 9.8995. The value 14 would be the rate per unit of the unnormalised direction, and it is larger because that direction is longer than one unit. A directional derivative is a rate per unit distance, so normalising the direction is not optional.
questions.hint: Compute the gradient at the point, then take its dot product with the unit direction.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a directional derivative in a given direction
questions.stem: Let f of x comma y comma z equal to x squared y, and let the direction be the unit vector 0.6 comma 0.8 comma 0. What is the directional derivative of f at the point (2, 3, 0) in that direction? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The partial derivatives are 2xy, x squared and 0, so the gradient at (2, 3, 0) is <12, 4, 0>. Dotting with the unit direction gives 12 times 0.6 plus 4 times 0.8, which is 7.2 + 3.2 = 10.4. The direction really is a unit vector, since 0.36 + 0.64 = 1, which is why no normalisation is needed here. Leaving out the third component would change nothing at this point only because that partial derivative happens to be zero, and it would matter at any point where z is not zero.
questions.hint: Take the dot product of the gradient at the point with the given unit direction.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: integrate a divergence to get net outflow
questions.stem: A two-dimensional flow has field F of x comma y equal to <2, 3y>. What is the net outward flow across the boundary of the rectangle whose corners are (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 2) and (0, 2)? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The divergence is the sum of the partial derivatives of the components, which is 0 + 3y, and the total net outflow is the integral of that over the rectangle. The constant part contributes 2 times the area 6, which is 12, and the varying part contributes 3 times the integral of y over the rectangle, and that integral is the width 3 times 2, which is 6, so 18. The total is 30. A figure of 10 comes from integrating in y alone and forgetting that x has width 3, while 19.5 comes from treating the rectangle as though it were a single vertical strip of unit width.
questions.hint: Differentiate each component with respect to its own coordinate, add, then integrate over the whole region.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute one component of a curl
questions.stem: A field is F of x comma y comma z equal to <y squared, x, 0>. What is the third component of the curl of F at the point (1, 2, 0)? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The third component of the curl is the partial derivative of the second component with respect to x minus the partial derivative of the first component with respect to y, which is 1 minus 2y, and at y = 2 that is 1 - 4 = -3. The other two components involve the third component of the field, which is the constant 0, and both come out zero because the field has no dependence on z at all. The common slip is to forget the constant 1 in the first partial derivative and report -4, which corresponds to differentiating only the squared term.
questions.hint: The third component of a curl is d of the second component over dx minus d of the first over dy.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the dot product of a field with a unit tangent
questions.stem: A curve is the circle x squared plus y squared equals 4, travelled counterclockwise, and the field acting along it is F of x comma y comma z equal to <y, -x, 0>. What is the value of F dotted with the unit tangent at the point where the angle is 0.3 radians? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: On the circle of radius 2 the point is <2 cos theta, 2 sin theta>, so the field there is <2 sin theta, -2 cos theta>, and the unit tangent for counterclockwise travel is <-sin theta, cos theta>. Their dot product is -2 sin squared theta minus 2 cos squared theta, which is -2 for every angle, so the 0.3 does not affect it. The value is a constant negative because the field turns the opposite way to the direction of travel, so a small step along the curve always moves against the field.
questions.hint: Write the field and the unit tangent at the same angle, then dot them and simplify.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to y
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a line integral built from dy
questions.stem: A path is the unit circle x squared plus y squared equal to 1, travelled once counterclockwise from the point (1, 0). What is the value of the integral of x with respect to y around that closed path? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Writing the path as x = cos theta and y = sin theta gives dy = cos theta d theta, so the integral becomes the integral from 0 to 2pi of cos squared theta, which is pi, about 3.1416. Green's theorem confirms it in one line: the integrand is just x, so the relevant partial derivative is 1 and the integral is the area of the disk, which is pi. The tempting zero comes from integrating sin theta instead, which would be the integral of y rather than the integral of x with respect to y.
questions.hint: Differentiate the parametrisation and watch which of x or y carries the d theta.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to x
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a line integral built from dx
questions.stem: A cable runs along the path where y equals x, with x going from 0 to 1. What is the value of the integral of y cubed with respect to x along that cable? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Along the line y equals x the integrand y cubed becomes x cubed, and the integration is already with respect to x, so the value is the integral of x cubed from 0 to 1, which is one quarter. Because the variable of integration is x, no length factor is needed here. The instinct to multiply by the square root of 1 plus the slope squared belongs to an arc length integral, and including it would wrongly multiply this answer by the square root of 2.
questions.hint: Substitute the path equation into the integrand and integrate with respect to the given variable.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to arc length
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a line integral with respect to arc length
questions.stem: A wire carries a density of x + 2y along the path where y equals 3 - 2x, with x running from 0 to 2. What is the total density integrated along the wire? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Substituting the path gives a density of x + 2 of 3 - 2x, which is 6 - 3x, and the element of arc length along a straight path of slope -2 is the square root of 1 + 4 = 5 times dx. So the integral is the square root of 5 times the integral of 6 - 3x from 0 to 2, and that integral is 12 - 6 = 6, giving 6 times the square root of 5, about 13.4164. Omitting the length factor would give 6, which answers the different question of the integral of the density with respect to x.
questions.hint: The arc length element along a straight path is the square root of 1 plus the slope squared, times dx.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integral with respect to arc length
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a line integral with respect to arc length on a circle
questions.stem: A hoop carries a density of y squared along the circle x squared plus y squared equal to 4, traversed once. What is the density integrated around the whole hoop? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Write the circle as x = 2 cos theta and y = 2 sin theta, and note that the element of arc length is 2 d theta, so the integral is the integral of 4 sin squared theta times 2, which is 8 times the integral of sin squared theta over a full turn, that is 8 pi, about 25.1327. Symmetry reaches the same figure in one step: on a circle the average of y squared is half the radius squared, that is 2, and the circumference is 4 pi, so the product is 8 pi. Both routes agree, which is the useful check that the length factor was carried correctly.
questions.hint: Parametrise the circle and remember that its arc length element is the radius times d theta.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a line integral of a field along a path
questions.stem: A field is F of x comma y equal to <2xy, x squared>, and a path is the curve where y equals x squared with x running from 0 to 1. What is the value of the integral of 2xy with respect to x plus x squared with respect to y along that path? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Along the path y = x squared we have dy = 2x dx, so the integral becomes the integral from 0 to 1 of 2x times x squared times dx plus x squared times 2x dx, which is 2x cubed plus 2x cubed, that is 4x cubed. Integrating gives x to the fourth at the upper end, which is 1. The two terms come from the two components of the field and neither can be dropped, since the first alone would give one half and the second alone would also give one half.
questions.hint: Differentiate the path equation to get the second differential, then integrate a single variable.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a circulation using Green's theorem
questions.stem: A field is F of x comma y equal to <-y, x>, and the curve is the unit square with corners (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 1) traversed counterclockwise. What is the circulation of the field around that boundary? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: For a counterclockwise boundary the circulation form of Green's theorem gives the integral of the partial derivative of the second component with respect to x minus the partial derivative of the first with respect to y, which is 1 minus negative 1, and that is 2 everywhere. The unit square has area 1, so the circulation is 2. Checking it edge by edge gives the same figure: the bottom and left edges contribute nothing, the right edge contributes 1 and the top edge contributes 1, for a total of 2.
questions.hint: Use the difference of the two crossed partial derivatives, then multiply by the area of the region.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the difference of two partial derivatives at a point
questions.stem: A field is F of x comma y equal to <y squared, x squared>. What is the value of the partial derivative of the second component with respect to x minus the partial derivative of the first component with respect to y, at the point (1, 0)? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The second component x squared differentiated with respect to x is 2x, and the first component y squared differentiated with respect to y is 2y, so the difference is 2x - 2y, which at (1, 0) is 2. The expression is not a constant: at the origin it is 0, and at (1, 1) it is again 0, so evaluating it at a stated point is essential. This quantity is the third component of the curl in two dimensions, and it feeds both the circulation and the flux versions of Green's theorem.
questions.hint: Differentiate each component with respect to the coordinate that names it, then substitute the point.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: recover an area from a closed line integral
questions.stem: A region is bounded by the curve y equals x squared, the x axis and the line x equals 2. What is the area of the region, if it is to be read off Green's theorem rather than computed by a single integral? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: One half of the closed integral of x with respect to y minus y with respect to x gives the area, and walking the boundary counterclockwise the edge along the x axis contributes nothing, the vertical edge at x = 2 contributes 2 times 4 = 8, and the curved edge from (2, 4) back to the origin contributes minus 8 over 3. Half of the total is 8 over 3, about 2.6667, which agrees with integrating x squared from 0 to 2 directly. The curved edge is the only place the calculus enters, and forgetting that a closed curve has no single starting point is a common way to lose track of the signs.
questions.hint: Use one half of the closed integral of x dy minus y dx, and walk each edge with its orientation.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a double integral over a rectangle
questions.stem: A double integral runs from 0 to 1 in x and from 0 to 1 in y, with integrand 2y + 3x. What is its value? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The integral separates into two pieces because the integrand is a sum: the integral of 2y with respect to y from 0 to 1 is 1, and the integral of 3x with respect to x from 0 to 1 is 1.5, and each of these is then integrated over the other variable without changing it. That gives 2.5. Evaluating the inner integral at one fixed value of the other variable would give a different figure, because the two terms depend on different variables and each must be integrated in its own.
questions.hint: Split the sum and integrate each term in the variable it actually depends on.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a double integral in the reverse order
questions.stem: The same double integral, with integrand 2y + 3x over the unit square, is now set up with y integrated first and x second. What value does the reversed setup give? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Reversing the order of integration cannot change the value, because the double integral is a genuine two-dimensional quantity and the two iterated forms are only two ways of computing it. Integrating 2y with respect to y first gives 1 as the inner value, which then integrates over x to give 1, and 3x is constant in y, so the inner integral is 3x and integrating over x gives 1.5. The total is again 2.5, which is the check that both setups describe the same region.
questions.hint: A region of integration keeps the same value when the order of integration is reversed.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute a double integral with reversed limits
questions.stem: A double integral of 2y + 3x is written over the unit square but with both pairs of limits subtracted in the reversed order, that is from 0 to 1 minus from 1 to 0 at each level. What is the value of the integral? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Reversing the limits of an integral changes its sign, since the integral from 1 to 0 of a function is the negative of the integral from 0 to 1. The two reversals are nested rather than side by side, so the sign change applies to the inner integral and the outer one at the same time, and the whole double integral is the negative of 2.5, that is -2.5. A negative value here does not describe a region of negative area; it describes the same square swept in the opposite sense, and reversing both pairs of limits again would return the positive answer.
questions.hint: Remember that an integral with its limits swapped picks up a minus sign.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Polar coordinates for a double integral
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a double integral in polar coordinates
questions.stem: A double integral of x squared plus y squared runs over the quarter disk in the first quadrant where x squared plus y squared is at most 1. What is its value? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: In polar coordinates the integrand becomes r squared and the area element brings another factor of r, so the integral is the integral from 0 to pi over 2 of the integral from 0 to 1 of r cubed, and the inner integral is 1 over 4, giving pi over 8, about 0.3927. Leaving out the Jacobian would give pi over 2, which is simply the area of the quarter disk with the integrand ignored, and using an angular range of 2pi would sweep the whole disk and give pi over 4, twice the correct value.
questions.hint: The integrand becomes r squared and the area element contributes a further factor of r.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Angular range in a polar integral
questions.learningObjective: diagnose the effect of a doubled angular range
questions.stem: A student sets up the integral of x squared plus y squared over the quarter disk in the first quadrant, but uses an angular range of 0 to 2pi while keeping the correct radius limits of 0 to 1. What value does that setup produce? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: With the radius limits correct the integrand is still r cubed, and integrating r cubed from 0 to 1 gives 1 over 4, so the only thing the wrong angular range changes is the size of the angular measure. Over 0 to 2pi that is 2pi instead of pi over 2, four times as much, so the value is 4 times pi over 8, that is pi over 4, about 0.7854. The setup is quietly integrating over the whole disk of radius 1 rather than its quarter, and since both figures are positive the size is the only clue that anything is wrong.
questions.hint: The radius limits are right, so work out how much the angular range over-counts.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a triple integral over a box
questions.stem: A triple integral of z squared runs over the box where x runs from 0 to 1, y from 0 to 1 and z from 0 to 2. What is the value of the integral? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Integrating z squared from 0 to 2 gives 2 cubed over 3, which is 8 over 3, and that value is then constant in x and y, so the remaining two integrations only contribute their lengths, 1 and 1. The total is 8 over 3, about 2.6667. The figure 16 over 3 is what appears if the unit lengths of the x and y intervals are each treated as 2, and a quick check is that the average value of z squared over a box is one third of the cube of the height, that is 8 over 3 out of a volume of 2.
questions.hint: Integrate the innermost variable first, then multiply by the lengths of the remaining two intervals.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a triple integral whose integrand varies
questions.stem: A triple integral of k minus k cubed runs where k runs from 0 to 1 and the other two variables each run over the unit interval. What is the value of the integral?

options.misconception: integrates only the linear term and drops the cubic one entirely
integrates each term in a single variable but forgets to add them
treats the two terms as though they cancelled rather than adding their integrals

questions.explanation: The integrand mentions only one of the three variables, so the other two integrations contribute 1 times 1 and the calculation reduces to the integral of k minus k cubed from 0 to 1, which is one half minus one quarter, that is 0.25. The integrand changes sign at the square root of one third, so the net figure is well below the integral of k alone, which is 0.5, and a setup that integrated the volume first would report 1 and lose the negative contribution altogether.
questions.hint: Integrate out the variables the integrand does not mention, then integrate what is left.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a line integral by finding a potential
questions.stem: A field is F of x comma y equal to <1, x>, and a path is the curve y equals x squared with x running from 0 to 1. What is the value of the integral of the first component with respect to x plus the second component with respect to y along that path?

options.misconception: integrates only the first component and drops the contribution of the second
treats the second differential as though it were the first and adds 1 to 1
integrates the second term correctly but forgets to add the contribution of the first

questions.explanation: The field is the gradient of the function f of x comma y equal to x plus x squared over 2, so the integral along any path is the change in f, and f at the end minus f at the start is (1 + 1 over 2) - 0 = 1.5. Substituting the path directly confirms it: with dy equal to 2x dx the integral becomes the integral of 1 plus 2x squared, which is 1 + 2 over 3, that is 1.6667, and the gap between the two figures is a reminder to check which form was actually integrated.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: find a potential and then apply the fundamental theorem
questions.stem: A field is F of x comma y equal to <2x, 2y>. First find a potential function whose gradient is that field, then report the change in that potential between the points (0, 0) and (3, 4). Report the number only.

options.misconception: adds the two endpoint values instead of subtracting the start from the finish
reports the straight-line distance between the two points rather than the change in potential
halves the result by stopping halfway through the change

questions.explanation: The potential is f equal to x squared plus y squared, since its partial derivatives are 2x and 2y, and the change in f between the two points is 25 - 0 = 25. That change is the line integral of the field along any path joining them, which is the content of the fundamental theorem for line integrals. Here the potential happens to be the square of the distance from the origin, so the change is just the square of the outer radius, and a student who reports 5 has computed that distance rather than its square.
questions.hint: Find the potential, then subtract its value at the start from its value at the finish.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the curvature of a path from the speed along it
questions.stem: A particle retraces a fixed curve but at twice the speed it used before. What has happened to the curvature of the path it travels along?

options.text: It is unchanged, since curvature depends on the shape of the path and not on the rate it is covered
It has doubled, since curvature measures how quickly the direction of travel changes each second
options.misconception: confuses the rate of turning with distance, so a faster traversal reads as more bending

options.text: It has halved, since the same turning is now spread over twice as much time
options.misconception: confuses the rate of turning per unit time with the rate of turning per unit distance

options.text: It is no longer defined, because curvature is only meaningful for a single speed
options.misconception: believes curvature is defined only for a particular speed of traversal

questions.explanation: Curvature measures how much the direction of travel turns per unit of distance travelled, so it is a property of the path itself and is unchanged by how fast the path is covered. Speeding up a traversal makes the direction turn faster per second, but it also covers more distance in that second, and the ratio of the two is exactly what curvature is. This is the same reason that constant-speed circular motion has constant curvature whatever the speed, and why a straight path has curvature zero at any speed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the turning is being measured per unit distance or per unit time.

Dropping the exponential while differentiating would leave a factor of the function value out of each partial derivative, which here would give 1 rather than 1 but would matter at any other point.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute a divergence and then a curl for one field
questions.stem: The field F of x comma y comma z equal to <2x, 3y, 4z> is to be examined at the point (1, 1, 1). First report its divergence, then report the magnitude of its curl. Report the number only.

options.misconception: adds the two requested quantities together instead of reporting the first of them
reports the difference of the two quantities rather than the first
answers only the second quantity and leaves the first unreported

questions.explanation: The divergence is the sum of the partial derivatives of the components, 2 + 3 + 4 = 9, and it is the same at every point because each component depends only on its own coordinate. The curl is zero everywhere, since differentiating 3y with respect to x and 2x with respect to y both give 0 and the other components are similarly unrelated. So the field expands without any local rotation, which is exactly the pattern of a field whose curl vanishes while its divergence does not.
questions.hint: Differentiate each component with respect to its own coordinate and add for the divergence, then do the crossed pairings for the curl.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: test a claim about a field using divergence and curl
questions.stem: A student claims that the field of <x, y, z> has a divergence equal to 3 everywhere and a curl that is never zero. First compute the divergence of that field, then report the magnitude of its curl at the origin. Report the number only.

options.misconception: believes the curl of a radial field vanishes only at the origin rather than everywhere
confuses the gradient of the squared radius with the curl of the field
accepts the student's claim and reports the sum of the two quantities instead

questions.explanation: The divergence of <x, y, z> is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, so the first half of the claim is right. The curl is zero at every point, because the crossed partial derivatives pair each coordinate with a different variable and each such pair differentiates to zero. So the second half of the claim is false and the field contradicts itself: it expands everywhere yet turns nowhere. The two quantities measure independent things, a source strength and a local rotation, and either can be nonzero while the other vanishes.
questions.hint: Compute both quantities before judging the claim, and do the crossed partial derivative pairings carefully.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: choose the correct polar set-up for a double integral
questions.stem: A student needs the double integral of x over the disk x squared plus y squared less than or equal to 4, and wants to write it in polar coordinates. Which of the four set-ups is correct?

options.text: One half the integral of r cos theta times r, with theta from 0 to 2pi and r from 0 to 2
One half the integral of r cos theta alone, with theta from 0 to 2pi and r from 0 to 2
options.misconception: omits the Jacobian factor that the polar area element carries

options.text: One half the integral of r squared cos theta times r, with theta from 0 to 2pi and r from 0 to 2
options.misconception: squares the radius as though the integrand were x squared rather than x

options.text: The integral of r cos theta times r, with theta from 0 to 2pi and r from 0 to 2 and no one half
options.misconception: believes a full angular turn already supplies the wedge-area factor of one half

questions.explanation: The integrand x becomes r cos theta in polar coordinates and the element of area is r dr d theta, so the integrand times the area element is r squared cos theta, with the extra factor of r and the factor of one half for the thin wedge. Only the first set-up has both, and it evaluates to 0, which is what symmetry demands: the integrand is odd in x and the disk is symmetric, so no positive value can be correct. The fourth set-up has the Jacobian but no one half, and would report twice the value.
questions.hint: The integrand becomes r cos theta and the area element brings a factor of r on top of it.

questions.learningObjective: diagnose an unverified path independence claim
questions.stem: A student integrates the field of negative y in the first slot and x in the second, along both the unit circle and the diameter from (0, 0) to (1, 0), then claims the two answers must agree because the paths have the same shape. Where is the reasoning wrong?

options.text: The two paths have different endpoints, so path independence was never in question for them
The field is conservative, so the two values must agree and the student is right to expect it
options.misconception: believes every planar field is the gradient of a potential and so has path independence

options.text: Path independence holds for every field, so the claim is valid and the two values are equal
options.misconception: believes path independence is a property of all fields rather than of some

options.text: A closed curve cannot serve as a path for a line integral, so only the diameter contributes
options.misconception: believes a closed curve is not a legitimate path for a line integral

questions.explanation: The fundamental theorem for line integrals compares two paths that share both endpoints, and here the circle is closed, so it runs from (1, 0) back to (1, 0), while the diameter runs from (0, 0) to (1, 0). Different endpoints mean the theorem simply does not apply, and the field is not conservative in any case, since the mixed partial derivatives do not agree. The two values are 2 pi for the counterclockwise circle and one half for the diameter, and no contradiction follows because they answer different questions about different pairs of points.
questions.hint: Check whether the two paths share a starting point and a finishing point.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a disk method used where the region is described against the other axis
questions.stem: A student needs the volume under z equal to 1 - x squared over the base between the curve y equals x squared and the x axis, with x running from 0 to 1, and writes the integral of pi times 1 minus x squared with respect to x. Which correction and reason is right?

options.text: Integrate with respect to y, because the base is given by y as a function of x, so slices perpendicular to the y axis are the disks
Keep the integral as written, because pi times a height is the area of a disk of that radius
options.misconception: believes a disk cross-section can be built from a height recorded against the wrong axis

options.text: Use the integral of 2 pi x times 1 minus x squared with respect to x, because a volume needs a radius
options.misconception: confuses the disk method with the shell method when choosing which axis to slice

options.text: Integrate the product of the two heights with respect to x, because the base and the top act together
options.misconception: believes the base curve and the top surface contribute multiplicatively rather than one slicing the other

questions.explanation: The base is the region between y = 0 and y = x squared, which is naturally described by y as a function of x, so slices perpendicular to the y axis are disks. At height y the base reaches from x = 0 out to x = the square root of y, so the disk radius is the square root of y and its area is pi y, and integrating that from 0 to 1 gives pi over 2, about 1.5708. Integrating pi times 1 minus x squared with respect to x treats the height as a radius measured from the x axis, which is a different solid altogether.
questions.hint: Look at how the base region is written down and slice along the axis it is expressed against.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: state the conditions a boundary must meet for Green's theorem
questions.stem: A region is bounded by a curve, and a field is smooth everywhere inside and on it. Before Green's theorem may be applied, what must be true of the boundary?

options.text: The boundary must be a simple closed curve traversed so that the region stays on the left
The boundary must be a circle, since no other shape gives a well-defined interior
options.misconception: believes Green's theorem is stated only for circular regions

options.text: The boundary must be smooth everywhere, since a straight edge breaks the hypotheses
options.misconception: believes straight edges on a boundary disqualify a region from the theorem

options.text: The boundary must be traversed exactly once in the clockwise sense, which fixes the sign
options.misconception: believes the clockwise orientation is the required rather than the counterclockwise one

questions.explanation: The theorem needs the region to have a well-defined interior, which is what a simple closed curve supplies, and it needs a stated orientation, with the counterclockwise traversal placing the region on the left as the curve is walked. Straight edges are perfectly acceptable, so smoothness of the boundary is not the requirement, and a self-intersecting curve is excluded because it encloses no single region. Naming a curve simple and closed is not enough on its own; each condition has to be checked against the actual path.
questions.hint: Ask whether the curve encloses one region unambiguously, and which way round it is being walked.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a reversed orientation
questions.stem: The field of negative y in the first slot and x in the second acts on the unit circle, which is traversed once clockwise. A student applies Green's theorem with the usual positive orientation and reports a circulation of 2. What is the correction?

options.text: The orientation is reversed, so the circulation is -2 rather than 2
The orientation makes no difference, since the theorem fixes the answer for a closed curve
options.misconception: believes Green's theorem carries no orientation requirement on the boundary

options.text: The orientation is reversed, so the circulation should be reported as 0
options.misconception: believes a reversed orientation cancels the integrand instead of negating it

options.text: The orientation is irrelevant here, but the correct value is 4 rather than 2
options.misconception: doubles the value in place of negating it

questions.explanation: Green's theorem for circulation reads the boundary integral as a double integral of a partial derivative difference, and it assumes the boundary is traversed so that the region stays on the left, which is counterclockwise. Traversing the same circle clockwise puts the region on the right, and every incremental contribution changes sign, so the circulation is -2 rather than 2. Checking it directly confirms the sign: with the clockwise parametrisation the integral of the field dotted with the displacement comes to -pi, the negative of the counterclockwise value.
questions.hint: Fix the orientation first, then decide whether the correction is a sign change or a change of theorem.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a swapped pair of partial derivatives
questions.stem: The planar field whose first component is y squared and whose second component is x squared is being analysed, and a student computes its single curl component as 2y - 2x before integrating it over a triangle. Which correction and reason is right?

options.text: The two partial derivatives are the same quantities subtracted in the other order, so the value is 2x - 2y
The order of subtraction does not matter, so the sign error leaves the result unchanged
options.misconception: believes the difference of two partial derivatives is independent of their order

options.text: Both partial derivatives should be taken with respect to the same coordinate variable
options.misconception: believes both partials in a two-dimensional curl use the same coordinate

options.text: The curl of a planar field has three components, so a single component is not defined
options.misconception: believes a field confined to the plane cannot be curled

questions.explanation: The third component of the curl is the partial derivative of the second component with respect to x minus the partial derivative of the first component with respect to y, and here that is 2x - 2y. The student has each partial derivative right but has subtracted the two in the wrong order, so the sign of the whole integrand flips and any signed line integral or flux it feeds is negated. Subtraction is not commutative, which is exactly why the definition fixes the order of the two terms.
questions.hint: Write the definition out in components before computing any of them.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the gradient points the way a scalar rises fastest
questions.stem: Explain why the gradient of a differentiable function points in the direction in which the function increases fastest, and say what its magnitude tells you.

answer.exemplar: For any unit direction u the directional derivative is the rate of change of the function when the point is displaced in the direction u, and the first-order approximation says that rate equals the gradient dotted with u. Because u has length one, that dot product cannot exceed the magnitude of the gradient, and equality holds exactly when u is parallel to the gradient, by the equality condition in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. So the direction of the gradient realises the largest possible rate, and the magnitude of the gradient is that largest rate per unit distance. A direction perpendicular to the gradient gives a zero directional derivative, and that is the level curve through the point, which is why level curves run across the gradient rather than along it.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to carry the inequality step, since the direction claim only follows once the unit-length constraint and the bound are both stated.
questions.hint: Express the directional derivative as a dot product and ask when that dot product is largest.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute a gradient and a divergence and label each output
questions.stem: The function f of x comma y equal to x cubed plus 2xy has a gradient, and the field F of x comma y equal to <x squared, 3y> has a divergence. What are those two quantities?

options.text: The gradient is <3x squared + 2y, 2x>, a vector, and the divergence is 2x + 3, a scalar
The gradient is 3x squared + 2y + 2x, a scalar, and the divergence is 2x + 3, a vector
options.misconception: adds the two partial derivatives together instead of collecting them as a vector

options.text: The gradient is <3x squared + 2y, 2x>, a scalar, and the divergence is 2x + 3, a vector
options.misconception: gets both expressions right but attaches the wrong output type to each one

options.text: The gradient is <3x squared + 2y, 2x>, a vector, and the divergence is x squared + 3y, a scalar
options.misconception: reads the components of the field straight off instead of differentiating each in turn

questions.explanation: Differentiating f with respect to x gives 3x squared + 2y and with respect to y gives 2x, and a gradient collects the partials as a vector. A divergence starts from the two components of the field, differentiates the first with respect to x to get 2x and the second with respect to y to get 3, and adds them into the single scalar 2x + 3. So one operator takes a scalar and returns a vector, the other takes a vector and returns a scalar, and the two results cannot be interchanged even where the formulas look superficially similar.
questions.hint: Ask how many numbers go into each operator and how many come out.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the claim that a curl-free field is a gradient
questions.stem: Explain what a vanishing curl of a vector field does and does not guarantee on a closed region, and say what extra assumption is needed before the field can be called conservative.

answer.exemplar: A vanishing curl says the field has no local tendency to rotate, that is the net contribution around an infinitesimal loop is zero. On a simply connected region, meaning one with no holes, that is enough to make the field the gradient of some scalar function, and then every closed line integral of the field is zero and every line integral depends only on its endpoints. The extra assumption matters, because on a region with a hole the conclusion can fail: the field of negative y in the first slot and x in the second has curl zero everywhere, yet its integral around the unit circle is 2 pi, and no potential exists, since the region enclosed by that circle is missing from the domain. The correct statement of the theorem is therefore local vanishing of the curl together with simple connectivity, not vanishing curl alone.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to state the connectivity hypothesis and give the counterexample that shows why it cannot be dropped.
questions.hint: Check whether a loop in the region can fail to shrink to a point.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain what path independence asserts and what it presumes
questions.stem: Explain what it means for a line integral of a vector field to be path independent, and state what must be verified before relying on it.

answer.exemplar: Path independence means the integral of the field along any curve joining the same two points has the same value, so the integral measures the difference between an endpoint quantity and itself rather than the route taken. Two things must be checked before relying on it. First, the paths must actually share both endpoints, since two routes between different pairs of points are not being compared at all. Second, and this is the step usually skipped, path independence must be established for the field rather than assumed: a field is conservative when a potential exists, which on a simply connected region is equivalent to the curl vanishing, and that has to be checked from the components. The field of negative y in the first slot and x in the second shows how easily the assumption is made wrongly, since all of its partial derivatives exist and yet the circulation around a circle is 2 pi rather than zero.

questions.explanation: The exemplar separates the endpoint condition from the field condition, since assuming the second is the standard error.
questions.hint: Write down what a path-independent integral would equal, and ask when that claim is licensed.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the polar area element gains a factor of r
questions.stem: Explain why a double integral written in polar coordinates picks up an extra factor of r in its area element, and what a computation without it actually measures.

answer.exemplar: A small change d theta at radius r sweeps a thin annular sector whose area is one half r squared d theta, so an element of area is a length times a width: the width is r d theta, because the arc subtended by a small angle grows in proportion to the radius. The extra factor of r is exactly that width, which is why a polar area element is r dr d theta. A computation that omits it is integrating the integrand against dr d theta, which has units of area per unit radius and so no longer measures an area at all. On the quarter disk of radius 1 the missing width averages one half, so a constant integrand would come out halved rather than merely wrong by an unknown factor, and a non-constant one is worse still because the error grows with radius.

questions.explanation: The exemplar derives the factor from the annular sector and then says what the omission amounts to dimensionally.
questions.hint: Find the area of a thin annular sector and read off which factor plays the role of the width.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute a gradient in three variables
questions.stem: A scalar field is f of x comma y comma z equal to x squared plus 2yz. What is the gradient of that field?

options.misconception: lists the partials in the order x, y, z regardless of which variable each belongs to
leaves the y partial unevaluated and then puts y in the wrong slot
divides every partial derivative by two instead of differentiating the squared term

questions.explanation: Differentiating with respect to x gives 2x, with respect to y gives 2z, and with respect to z gives 2y, and the gradient lists those three partials in that coordinate order, so it is <2x, 2z, 2y>. The y and z entries look transposed because the term 2yz is symmetric in those two variables, but each slot is fixed by which variable is being held fixed during the differentiation. Forgetting the factor of 2 from the squared term would leave <x, z, y>, which scales the x component wrongly.
questions.hint: Differentiate once with respect to each coordinate, holding the other two fixed.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: identify the direction of fastest increase and its rate
questions.stem: At a certain point the gradient of a function is <3, 4>. Which pair gives the direction of fastest increase there and the rate achieved in that direction?

options.text: The unit vector <3/5, 4/5>, at a rate of 5 per unit distance
The unit vector <3/5, 4/5>, at a rate of 25 per unit distance
options.misconception: reports the square of the gradient magnitude as the fastest rate of increase

options.text: The unit vector <4/5, 3/5>, at a rate of 5 per unit distance
options.misconception: swaps the two components of the direction while keeping the rate

options.text: The unit vector <1, 0>, at a rate of 3 per unit distance
options.misconception: picks the largest single component and treats it as the best direction

questions.explanation: The direction of fastest increase is the direction of the gradient itself, normalised, and the magnitude of <3, 4> is 5, so the unit direction is <3/5, 4/5> and the fastest rate is 5 per unit distance. The two go together, because the directional derivative along the unit vector parallel to the gradient equals the magnitude of the gradient by the equality condition in the standard inequality. Squaring the magnitude to get 25 would report a rate per unit area rather than per unit distance, and using only the larger component throws away the other one's contribution.
questions.hint: The direction is the gradient normalised and the rate is its magnitude, not its square.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute all three components of a curl
questions.stem: Consider the field F of x comma y comma z equal to <-y, z, 0>. What is the curl of that field?

options.misconception: gets the sign of the middle component wrong by a single derivative
negates all three components at once instead of following each pairing
keeps the right magnitudes but flips the sign of the third component

questions.explanation: The first component of the curl is the partial derivative of the third with respect to y minus the partial of the second with respect to z, which is 0 - 1 = -1. The second is the partial of the first with respect to z minus the partial of the third with respect to x, which is 0 - 0 = 0, and the third is the partial of the second with respect to x minus the partial of the first with respect to y, which is 0 minus negative 1, that is 1. So the curl is <-1, 0, 1>.
questions.hint: Write the three component formulas down in order and fill in each partial derivative.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: interpret what a nonzero curl reports
questions.stem: A three-dimensional field has a curl that is not zero at some point. What does that tell you about the field near that point?

options.text: The field circulates locally, so small loops around the point gather a net contribution
The field grows or drains locally, so the net flow through small boxes is nonzero
options.misconception: confuses the curl, which measures rotation, with the divergence, which measures expansion

options.text: The field has a direction of fastest increase there, which can be read off the curl
options.misconception: believes the curl of a field contains the direction of steepest ascent of a potential

options.text: The field cannot be the gradient of a potential, and nothing further can be said
options.misconception: believes ruling out a potential settles the matter and forecloses further analysis

questions.explanation: The curl measures local circulation, and by Stokes' theorem its component along a normal is the circulation around a small loop in that plane divided by the enclosed area, so a nonzero curl means small loops pick up a net contribution. That is a statement about turning rather than expansion, which is what the divergence reports, and the curl is a vector rather than the direction of steepest ascent of any potential. A nonzero curl does rule out the field being a gradient on a simply connected region, but the positive statement about local circulation is the more informative half.
questions.hint: Recall which small loops the curl measures the circulation around.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line integrals with respect to arc length
questions.learningObjective: interpret the integrand of an arc length line integral
questions.stem: An integral of f with respect to arc length runs along a wire. What does the value of that integral represent?

options.text: The total of f over the wire, a sum of a value at each point weighted by how much wire lies there
The average value of f over the wire, which happens to be the same as that total
options.misconception: believes the total and the average are the same quantity for an arc length integral

options.text: The rate at which f changes as the wire is traversed at unit speed
options.misconception: confuses a weighted total with a rate of change along the curve

options.text: The total of f over the projection of the wire onto the horizontal axis
options.misconception: believes the shape of the curve can be ignored and a projection used instead

questions.explanation: An integral with respect to arc length is a limiting sum in which each value of f is multiplied by a small length of wire, so the result is the total of f distributed along the wire, with a dense stretch contributing more than a sparse one. It is not an average, which would need dividing by the total length, and it is not a rate, since no time appears anywhere. The geometry of the wire still matters through the element of arc length, which is why the shape of the curve changes the answer even when f does not.
questions.hint: Think of the integral as a limiting sum of a value times a small piece of length.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a signed differential integral from an arc length integral
questions.stem: A field is F of x comma y equal to <2x, 3y>, and the integral of the first component with respect to x plus the second with respect to y is taken along a path. How does that integral differ from an integral of a single scalar with respect to arc length?

options.text: It accumulates a signed amount attached to the direction of travel, so reversing the path negates it
It accumulates a total that ignores direction, so reversing the path leaves it unchanged
options.misconception: believes a signed directional integral cannot possibly depend on the direction of traversal

options.text: It accumulates an amount measured per unit length rather than per unit parameter
options.misconception: confuses an integral built from dx and dy with one built from ds

options.text: It accumulates the same total as the arc length version for every path and every field
options.misconception: believes the two integral types are interchangeable whenever the field is smooth

questions.explanation: In an integral of the form M dx + N dy each piece carries a sign that depends on which way the path is travelled, because dx and dy are themselves signed. Reversing the traversal swaps the signs of both differentials, so the whole integral changes sign. An integral with respect to arc length is made of unsigned lengths, so reversing the traversal leaves it alone, and that asymmetry is the practical test for telling the two kinds apart when a conservative field makes them agree on a closed loop.
questions.hint: Ask whether each piece of the integrand can be negative for some direction of travel.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Green's theorem and the region boundary
questions.learningObjective: relate a closed boundary integral to a double integral
questions.stem: A region has a simple closed boundary and a field is smooth everywhere inside and on it. What does Green's theorem convert the boundary integral into?

options.text: A double integral over the region of a combination of the field's partial derivatives
A double integral over the boundary itself, using a different area element
options.misconception: believes the region and its boundary are integrated over in the same way

options.text: A line integral along a diameter of the region, split into its two halves
options.misconception: believes a closed boundary has to be opened up along a diameter before use

options.text: A triple integral over the solid that the region bounds, using its thickness
options.misconception: believes Green's theorem adds a dimension and produces a volume

questions.explanation: Green's theorem trades the boundary of a planar region for the region itself: a circulation integral becomes the double integral of the difference of the two crossed partial derivatives, and a flux integral becomes the double integral of the divergence. The boundary and the region are one-dimensional and two-dimensional respectively, so the change of dimension is exactly what makes the theorem useful. Nothing about the theorem produces a volume, and the boundary is integrated along rather than over.
questions.hint: Compare the dimension of the boundary with the dimension of the region it encloses.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: interpret a double integral of a height
questions.stem: A double integral of a nonnegative function over a region in the plane gives a number. Under what condition does that number read as a volume?

options.text: Whenever the function is read as a height above the region, since the integral is then the volume beneath the surface
Never, since a double integral always produces an area and gains no dimension
options.misconception: believes a double integral cannot acquire a third dimension at all

options.text: Only when the region is a circle, since only then does the surface close up neatly
options.misconception: believes the shape of the base region restricts how the value may be read

options.text: Only when the function is constant, since only a flat surface has a definite volume
options.misconception: believes a volume requires the height to be constant across the whole base

The shape of the base region is irrelevant to that reading, and the height need not be constant, since a sloping surface above a flat base still encloses a volume. The same integral also reads as a mass with a density or as an area with a surface density, and the numerical value does not change, only what it stands for.

questions.topic: Recognising a region from its limits

questions.stem: An iterated integral runs from 0 to 1 in x on the outside and from 0 to x on the inside. Which region does it cover?

Reversing the order would describe the mirror region above the line, and the two together would make the square.

questions.topic: What two parameters imply on a surface
questions.learningObjective: interpret two parameters on a parametric surface
questions.stem: A rule r of u comma v equal to <u + v, u - v, 2v> with both parameters running from 0 to 1 is said to describe a patch. Why does the patch have area rather than only length?

questions.topic: Magnitude and direction of a vector

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a gradient from a directional derivative
questions.stem: A student has computed both the gradient of a function and a directional derivative of that same function. What distinguishes the two quantities?

The gradient is a scalar and a directional derivative is a vector, and the two are never related

options.text: The gradient depends only on the point while a directional derivative also depends on the path taken to reach it
options.misconception: believes a directional derivative carries extra information about the route to the point

options.text: The two are the same quantity in different notation, with the gradient being a shorthand
options.misconception: believes the gradient is only a notational convenience for a single directional rate

questions.explanation: The gradient is the vector of all partial derivatives, and each directional derivative is the gradient dotted with a unit direction, so the gradient packs every directional rate at that point into one vector. A single directional derivative is one scalar and depends on the direction chosen, whereas the gradient depends only on the point. The direction of the gradient is the special direction giving the largest of these scalars, and that relationship is the one worth carrying away from the pair.
questions.hint: Ask how many numbers each quantity has and how many directions each one accounts for.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: A curl and a divergence that contradict
questions.learningObjective: test a claim about a field using two operators
questions.stem: A student claims that a field has a divergence of 3 everywhere and a curl of 1 everywhere. What has to be established before any part of that claim can be relied on?

options.text: Both quantities must be computed from the components, since they measure unrelated things and either can hold while the other fails
Only the divergence matters, because a field with a nonzero divergence cannot have a nonzero curl
options.misconception: believes a nonzero divergence rules out a nonzero curl everywhere at once

options.text: Only the curl matters, because a field with a nonzero curl cannot have a nonzero divergence
options.misconception: believes a nonzero curl rules out a nonzero divergence everywhere at once

options.text: Nothing needs checking, since any pair of values is possible for a smooth field
options.misconception: believes the two operators are linked by a fixed identity allowing any pair of values

questions.explanation: The two operators measure independent things, expansion on the one hand and local rotation on the other, so no identity ties a value of one to a value of the other. A field can expand without turning, as <2x, 3y, 4z> does with divergence 9 and curl 0, or turn without expanding, as the rigid rotation field <-y, x, 0> does, and it can do both at once. So each claim has to be verified from the components, and checking only one of them establishes nothing about the other.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two operators are algebraically related to one another at all.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: state what the flux form of Green's theorem converts a boundary integral into
questions.stem: A field is smooth on a simple region and the boundary is traversed counterclockwise. What does the flux form of Green's theorem turn the outward flux integral around that boundary into?

options.text: The double integral of the divergence of the field over the region
The double integral of the difference of the two crossed partial derivatives
options.misconception: confuses the flux form with the circulation form, which uses crossed partials

options.text: The line integral of the field along a diameter of the region, split in two
options.misconception: confuses the change of dimension with an opening of the boundary along a diameter

options.text: The double integral of the curl of the field over the region
options.misconception: confuses the divergence with the curl, which measures rotation rather than outflow

questions.explanation: The flux form states that the outward flux across a counterclockwise boundary equals the double integral of the divergence over the region, and the divergence is the sum of the partial derivatives of the components, one rate of expansion per unit volume. The double integral of the difference of the crossed partial derivatives belongs to the circulation form, and the curl does not enter the flux form at all. Since both forms integrate the boundary and produce a double integral over the region, they are easy to confuse, and the way to keep them apart is to ask whether the quantity wanted is outflow or turning.
questions.hint: Decide whether the quantity being computed is net outflow or net turning, then pick the operator.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: find a potential function by integration
questions.stem: Which of the following is a potential function whose gradient equals the field F of x comma y equal to <2x, 2y>?

options.text: f of x comma y equal to x squared plus y squared
f of x comma y equal to 2x squared plus 2y squared
options.misconception: forgets the factor of one half that integration introduces on a linear term

options.text: f of x comma y equal to x squared minus y squared
options.misconception: drops the sign that the second component of the field requires

options.text: f of x comma y equal to 2x plus 2y
options.misconception: integrates without multiplying by the coordinate, so the result comes out linear

questions.explanation: A potential must differentiate to the given field, so the partial with respect to x should be 2x, and the integral of 2x with respect to x is x squared. The same holds in y, giving f equal to x squared plus y squared, up to an additive constant that the gradient cannot detect. The first distractor has partials 4x and 4y, which is the field doubled; the third has partials 2x and -2y, wrong in the second component; and the fourth is linear where the field is not.
questions.hint: Integrate one component with respect to its coordinate and then check the other component.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: choose a field whose boundary integral gives an area
questions.stem: A region is bounded on the left by the line y equals 3x, on the right by the line x equals 1, and below by the x axis. Which field makes the boundary integral equal to the area of the region directly?

options.text: The field with first component 0 and second component x, whose integrand becomes 1 around a counterclockwise boundary
The field with first component negative y and second component x, whose integrand becomes 2
options.misconception: uses the circulation field without the extra factor of one half that an area needs

options.text: The field with first component x and second component 0, whose integrand becomes 1
options.misconception: believes only the first component of the field can contribute to the area formula

options.text: The field with first component y and second component negative x, whose integrand becomes 2
options.misconception: reverses the signs of the circulation field without adjusting the prefactor

questions.explanation: The area of a region equals the integral around its counterclockwise boundary of P dx + Q dy when the partial derivative of Q with respect to x minus the partial of P with respect to y is 1, and taking the first component as 0 and the second as x makes exactly that difference equal to 1. The circulation field gives 2, so the same integral is twice the area unless a factor of one half is supplied, and reversing the signs makes the integrand -1 and the result minus the area. The region here is a triangle of base 1 and height 3, so the correct set-up must return 3 over 2.
questions.hint: Choose the two components so that the difference of the crossed partial derivatives is exactly 1.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a directional derivative in two variables
questions.stem: A function is f of x comma y equal to x squared plus y squared, and the direction is the unit vector with both components equal to 1 over the square root of 2. What is the directional derivative of f in that direction at the point (2, 1)?

options.misconception: reports the rate per unit of the unnormalised direction instead of per unit distance
divides the gradient dot product by the length of the direction a second time
drops one of the two partial derivatives before taking the dot product

questions.explanation: The gradient of f is <2x, 2y>, which at (2, 1) is <4, 2>, and dotting with the unit direction gives (4 + 2) over the square root of 2, that is 3 times the square root of 2, about 4.2426. The direction is genuinely a unit vector since each component squared is one half, so nothing needs normalising first. The value 6 is the rate per unit of the unnormalised direction <1, 1>, which is longer than one unit and therefore overstates the rate per unit distance.
questions.hint: Take the dot product of the gradient at the point with the unit direction.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: build a resultant and then normalise it
questions.stem: Two displacement vectors are <3, 4> and <-1, 0>. What is the second component of the unit vector that points along their resultant?

options.misconception: normalises only the first vector and then adds the second component unchanged
divides each component by the sum of the two components instead of the magnitude
assumes the unit vector along a resultant of these vectors must end in 1

questions.explanation: The resultant is <3 - 1, 4 + 0> = <2, 4>, whose magnitude is the square root of 4 + 16 = the square root of 20, so the unit vector is <2, 4> over the square root of 20 and its second component is 4 over the square root of 20, which is 0.8944. The value 0.8 comes from normalising the first vector alone, since 4 over 5 is 0.8, and that answers a different question because the two vectors are not parallel and the second one shifts the heading.
questions.hint: Add the vectors componentwise first, then divide every component by the magnitude of the resultant.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Recovering a function from a derivative
questions.learningObjective: recover a function from a known partial derivative
questions.stem: A function f is known to satisfy the partial derivative of f with respect to x equal to 6x. What is the value of f at the point (2, 0) if f is known to be 4 at the origin? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Integrating 6x with respect to x gives 3x squared plus a constant, and the constant is 4 because the function takes the value 4 at the origin. At x = 2 the value is 3 times 4 plus 4, that is 16. Integrating rather than differentiating is the step that catches people here, since a partial derivative pins a function down only up to a constant and up to any dependence on the other variable, and the single value at one point is what fixes both of those.
questions.hint: Antiderivative first, then use the value at the origin to fix the constant.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a double integral by reading it as a volume
questions.stem: A solid sits under the surface z equal to 1 - x over the triangular base where x runs from 0 to 1 and y from 0 to 1 - x. What is its volume? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Read the double integral as a volume, with the height 1 - x above each point of the base. Integrating 1 - x with respect to y from 0 to 1 - x gives (1 - x) squared, and then integrating that from 0 to 1 gives one third, about 0.3333. The tempting shortcut is to multiply the base area of one half by the height at the origin, which gives one half, but the height falls as x rises while the base narrows at the same time, so the solid is thinner exactly where the base is widest and the simple product is not a volume at all.
questions.hint: Integrate the height with respect to the inner variable first, keeping the limits.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Polar coordinates for a double integral
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a polar double integral over a disk
questions.stem: A double integral of x squared runs over the whole disk of radius 1 centred at the origin. What is its value? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: In polar coordinates the integrand becomes r squared cos squared theta and the area element brings another factor of r, so the integral is the integral from 0 to 2pi of the integral from 0 to 1 of r cubed cos squared theta, and the two parts separate into 1 over 4 and pi. The product is pi over 4, about 0.7854. Symmetry gives the same answer in one step: x squared and y squared have the same integral over a symmetric disk, and their sum is 1 everywhere on the disk, so each must account for half of pi.
questions.hint: The integrand becomes r squared times cos squared theta and the area element contributes a further r.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: identify a volume and then evaluate its double integral
questions.stem: A solid sits under the surface z equal to 2 - y over the base given by 0 at most x at most 1 and 0 at most y at most 1. First report the value of the surface at the corner (0, 0), then report the volume of the solid. Report the number only.

options.misconception: forgets that the height falls as y rises and integrates the corner value throughout
doubles the corner value and then divides the base area the wrong way round
adds the corner value to the volume instead of averaging the height over the base

questions.explanation: At the corner (0, 0) the surface gives 2, and the volume is the double integral of 2 - y over the unit square, which separates into the integral of 2 over the square, that is 2, minus the integral of y, that is one half. So the volume is 1.5, which is the base area of 1 times the average height of 1.5. Reporting 2 would treat the whole square as though it sat at the corner height, overstating the volume, since the surface slopes down towards y = 1 where it reaches 1.
questions.hint: Evaluate the height at the corner, then integrate the height over the square.
